title: Microsoft Was The Only Big AI Buyer Paying Down Debt. How Much More Can It Spend? - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks? Microsoft nearly doubled its capital spending in the year to June 2026. Capital spending is money put into long-lived assets, such as data centers. Even so, Microsoft had cash left over. Friday, Nov 20, was a hard day for AI stocks. Nvidia fell 14.0%, a chip-stock fund (SMH) 10.6% and the Nasdaq 100 fund (QQQ) 5.7%. Microsoft fell 2.8%, less than the S&P 500 fund (SPY), which lost 3.6%. Source: Microsoft’s cash-flow statements, fiscal years ending June 30. “Left over” is cash brought in minus capital spending, buybacks and dividends. A negative “borrowed” means it repaid more debt than it took on. Microsoft’s capital spending reached $116 billion in its last fiscal year, up from $65 billion. It still paid shareholders nearly $49 billion. It also paid down $3 billion of debt. Every other big AI buyer borrowed in the year to September. Microsoft repaid. Then, on Nov. 4, it sold $25 billion of new bonds. Its interest bill last fiscal year was $3.1 billion. That was less than the $3.3 billion it earned on its cash. The latest quarter, to September, shows the pace rising. Microsoft spent $39.4 billion against $58.0 billion brought in. We follow the other big builders’ cash in Big Tech Earned $607 Billion. Where Did It Go? Microsoft nearly doubled its capital spending and still paid its shareholders nearly $49 billion. If you want your savings to pay you an income, that kind of cash is what to look for. The Trefis Income Solution owns 50 companies that have each paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row, and together they yield about 3 times what the S&P 500 pays. See the Income Solution. Analysts expect sales of $396 billion in the year to June 2027, or fiscal 2027. Microsoft turns about 57 cents of every $1 of sales into cash. On those sales, that is about $224 billion. Source: Trefis. Sales are the consensus of 37 analysts. Cash is 56.5% of sales, the past four quarters’ rate. Dividends are at the latest quarter’s rate. Debt is borrowed debt at Sep 30, $35.5 billion, without leases. Buybacks are not counted. Keeping them would cut the room by about $18 billion. That last line is what sets Microsoft apart. Its debt at Sep 30 was about a sixth of a year’s cash. It could borrow $188 billion before its debt equaled a year of cash. That is more room than Alphabet ($117 billion) or Meta ($89 billion). The Nov. 4 bond sale leaves about $163 billion of room. We run the same numbers for Meta in Meta Stopped Its Buybacks To Build AI. How Much More Can It Spend? About $21 billion from Microsoft’s own cash, and up to $119 billion if it borrows. Nvidia‘s sales equal about 52 cents of every $1 the five biggest buyers spend. On that yardstick, Microsoft’s $39 billion of room is worth about $21 billion to Nvidia. With borrowing, the room is $228 billion, worth about $119 billion to Nvidia. Analysts’ forecast for Nvidia has about $118 billion that no buyer’s cash or borrowing room covers yet. That gap already counts Microsoft borrowing to its limit. The line to remember: Microsoft nearly doubled its capital spending last fiscal year and still repaid debt. It has the most room to borrow of any buyer, even after its November bond sale. In our view, a company that pays for its growth from its own cash is a sign of quality. Owning many such companies means you do not depend on just one. title: Hank Paulson Has “Never Seen So Much Money Chasing One Opportunity.” That’s a Problem for Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet - TIKR.com
content: da-kuk from Getty Images Signature and  CG6 Images from Getty Images via Canva Hank Paulson ran the Treasury through the 2008 crisis, so when he calls a boom dangerous, I listen. On Nov. 17, he told Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World: “I’ve never seen so much money chasing one opportunity with not a lot of earnings and ROI backing it up.” Microsoft (MSFT), Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOG) and Meta Platforms (META) are among the biggest spenders. Meta’s capex outran its operating cash in the third quarter, its first negative free cash flow quarter since 2012. In Bank of America’s November fund manager survey, 52% expect an AI hyperscaler to announce a capex cut within six months. That could hit suppliers like Arista Networks (ANET), which has named Microsoft and Meta as its two largest customers (42% of 2025 revenue). With revenue climbing, free cash flow is the better test of whether AI pays off. Amazon spent $131.8 billion on capex in 2025, or 94% of its $139.5 billion of operating cash flow. Its own free cash flow measure shows a $42.4 billion outflow in the 12 months to Sept. 30. Microsoft’s free cash flow has fallen two years running, even as revenue grew 18% in fiscal 2026, to $331.8 billion. Operating cash flow rose $46.8 billion that year and cash capex rose $51.4 billion, so the whole gain went into the build-out. Analysts expect fiscal 2027’s free cash flow to fall by about half, to $32.7 billion. Alphabet’s free cash flow held up in 2025, rising $0.5 billion to $73.3 billion as capex jumped to $91.4 billion from $52.5 billion. Then it turned negative: outflows widened from $5.9 billion in the June quarter to $9.1 billion in September. Microsoft’s commercial remaining performance obligation reached $678 billion at June 30, up 84%, and CFO Amy Hood said it grew 25% excluding OpenAI. But a backlog turns into cash over years, and the bills come due now. TIKR Tracks 58 Analysts on Microsoft. How Many Say “Buy”? If a hyperscaler announces the cut fund managers expect, I’d read it as good news for its shareholders. That goes double for Meta, where ads remain the main way to earn back its AI spending. Suppliers could take the hit. Arista grew third-quarter revenue 58.5% to $3.66 billion and guided to $3.9 billion to $4.0 billion for the fourth. With 42% of 2025 sales from those two, a cut to either’s networking orders could weigh on revenue. Until free cash flow grows again, these three are asking shareholders to take the AI payoff on faith. I wouldn’t pay up for any of them until the cash or the capex moves. Microsoft’s backlog could turn into cash faster than analysts expect. Its December-quarter report is the first test: free cash flow well above the $5.9 billion from a year earlier would start to answer Paulson. title: Microsoft (MSFT) Stock Price Prediction: Pullback tests support as analysts stay constructive - Blockchain News
content: Microsoft (MSFT) closed at $487.31, down 0.98% on the day and sitting just above the lower Bollinger Band at $487.67. The move comes after a strong first-quarter update on October 28 and a fresh ro... Microsoft (MSFT) is trading through a short-term pullback rather than a broken thesis. The stock’s last reported close was $487.31, with a 24-hour range of $504.49 to $481.86. That leaves MSFT below its 7-day, 20-day and 50-day moving averages, but still above its 200-day average of $463.48, which keeps the longer-term trend intact even as momentum has cooled. The company’s first-quarter results, announced on October 28, were the clearest fundamental anchor in the tape. Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19%, operating income of $45.9 billion, up 21%, and diluted earnings per share of $4.92 on a GAAP basis, up 32%. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion and accelerated to 30% growth, which is the kind of top-line and margin mix that helps explain why analysts have stayed supportive despite the recent share-price fade. Wall Street sentiment in the evidence set remains constructive. Stockanalysis.com cited 58 analysts with a consensus rating of Strong Buy and an average target of $636.12. Options Analysis Suite showed the November 2026 count at 58 analysts as well, with 12 Strong Buy, 41 Buy, 5 Hold and no Sell ratings, and an average target of $617.36 with a median of $630.00. Recent notes also remained supportive. RBC Capital maintained its Outperform rating and $640 target on November 20. TD Cowen reiterated Buy with a $650 target on November 18, while Guggenheim, J.P. Morgan and Mizuho were all in the $625 to $630 range on November 18. The read-through is straightforward: analysts are still pricing in room for upside, but not because the stock is cheap in a vacuum. They are leaning on Microsoft’s cloud and AI execution. The technical profile is mixed to weak in the short term. MSFT’s daily RSI is 33.41, which is near oversold territory but not a full reversal signal on its own. The MACD reading is negative at -8.3726, and the stochastic oscillator is deeply depressed, with %K at 8.14 and %D at 6.51. That combination usually signals downside exhaustion is possible, but it does not confirm a turn. The moving-average structure is still bearish in the near term, with the 7-day average at $506.00 below the 20-day at $520.71 and the 50-day at $526.36. At the same time, the price is hugging the lower Bollinger Band at $487.67, and %B is slightly negative at -0.0054, which suggests MSFT is pressing into support rather than drifting comfortably below it. The key takeaway: this is a test of support, not a collapse. Immediate support sits at $477.95, with stronger support at $468.59. On the upside, the first resistance is $500.58, followed by stronger resistance at $513.85. The pivot point is $491.22, so the stock is essentially trading around a decision zone rather than in free fall. Daily ATR(14) is $16.20, which means the name can easily move enough in a session to revisit either support or resistance without a major change in the underlying story. The low-volume pullback regime, at 0.12x versus the five-day average, also argues that the decline has been more of a controlled de-risking than an aggressive liquidation. On Binance perpetual futures, the funding rate is neutral at 0.0000%, while open interest fell 4.57% over 24 hours to 42,990.27 contracts. The global long/short ratio was 0.7271, with 42.1% long and 57.9% short, and top-trader accounts were similarly skewed at 42.0% long and 58.0% short. That leans cautious, but it does not by itself prove a durable bearish call. At the same time, taker flow was bid-heavy, with a taker buy/sell ratio of 1.4865, implying stronger aggressive buying than selling in the latest 1-hour window. In plain terms, derivatives positioning looks defensive while intraday order flow has been more supportive. That split often shows up when price is probing support and traders are waiting for confirmation. A recovery above $500.58 would be the first clean sign that buyers are regaining control after the pullback. A move through $513.85 would matter more because it would start to unwind the bearish short-term moving-average structure and push MSFT back toward the $520 to $526 zone where the 20-day and 50-day averages sit. On the downside, a decisive break of $477.95 would leave $468.59 as the next major support area. That would also put the stock farther away from its 200-day average and weaken the case that this is just a mean-reversion reset. For now, Microsoft (MSFT) looks like a fundamentally strong large-cap that is working through a technical air pocket, with analyst targets still pointing higher but the chart needing proof. title: Tech Outages At Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) And Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) Cast Shadow Over Mullin's Global Threat Testimony - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 20, 2026 | Featured, News & Analysis, Politics A cascading wave of widespread technology failures at some of America’s largest companies has set an uneasy backdrop for high-stakes congressional oversight hearings in Washington. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is facing pointed questioning from lawmakers on Capitol Hill over the administration’s assessment of worldwide security threats. The timing of his appearance has drawn heightened scrutiny given the recent rash of major outages that disrupted services across Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), and several major airline networks. Those failures have renewed urgent questions about the resilience of critical digital infrastructure and whether the country’s technology backbone is adequately protected against both accidental and deliberate disruption. Space Force chief software officer Nicolas Chaillan weighed in on the situation, offering his perspective on the wave of tech failures and what they signal about broader systemic vulnerabilities. Chaillan’s comments underline a growing concern among defense and security professionals that widespread outages, regardless of their origin, expose dangerous fragility in systems that underpin everyday life. Airline networks were among the most visible casualties of the disruptions, with passengers facing delays and service interruptions that rippled across the broader transportation sector. For Mullin, the outages represent an unavoidable talking point as he confronts legislators eager to probe whether the federal government has a credible plan to prevent or respond to large-scale infrastructure failures. The convergence of a global threat briefing with fresh evidence of domestic technological fragility is likely to shape the tone and focus of the committee’s line of questioning considerably. Capitol Hill hearings on national security have increasingly expanded their scope to include cyber resilience and the private sector’s role in safeguarding infrastructure that millions of Americans depend on daily. The Mullin testimony arrives at a moment when policymakers are under pressure to demonstrate that oversight mechanisms can keep pace with the speed and scale of modern technological disruption. Whether the recent outages were the result of technical failures, cyberattacks, or some combination of both remains a central question that lawmakers are expected to press Mullin to answer directly. David Prior is a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, covering everything from current affairs and global politics to stock market news and analysis.

"How much you should have in reserves, whether you have a spouse or significant other or life partner that's helping with taking care of some of those expenses, should things go longer than expected." "Taxes play a major part in it as well," he adds. "The last thing you want is for the taxes to be paid, but you're still significantly short, because this lump sum number threw you into a new tax bracket." You should also think about the state of the company before making a decision. "The person who's best qualified to answer that is the person who's been in the kitchen to see how the sausage is made," said Lee. "Is your department returning a profit? Are you seeing young people being hired into your department? You have to put your CEO hat on and really determine, you know, is my department needed?" In some cases, it might be tempting to pivot your retirement plans if you get a buyout offer. In April 2026, for example, Microsoft offered a voluntary retirement package to certain employees whose years of service and age added up to 70 or more. But Lee says you should be cautious about changes to your retirement, especially when it comes to healthcare. "Health insurance can cost you upwards of over $2,000 a month for a couple in their 60s," he says. "Make sure that's included in your budget to help bridge you to Medicare, which is age 65." Before adjusting your retirement date, Lee says you'd be wise to make sure you'll actually reach the goals you've been working toward throughout your career. "Get an updated plan," he says. title: What Could Stall Microsoft Stock’s Run? - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks? Microsoft (MSFT) stock returned 19.4% over the six months to November 19, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 3.1%. The shares still closed 10.2% below their November 4 high. Bulls can point to a cloud business where buyers keep coming. But management itself sounded a note of caution on the October 28 earnings call. So what could slow Microsoft’s cloud down? Microsoft stock has already given back 10.2% since its November 4 high. If a big part of your savings is in this one stock, a deeper drop after a slow quarter would be hard to sit through. When the market has fallen, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has lost about 81 cents for every $1 its benchmark lost, on average. See the HQ record. Microsoft’s problem is supply, not buyers. “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply,” management said on the fiscal Q1 2027 call. Some computing capacity that outside suppliers were due to deliver in that quarter was delayed. Some contracts to rent chips from those suppliers have now slipped to the second half of the fiscal year. That is the first half of calendar 2027. That delay makes Microsoft’s own forecast harder to hit. Azure revenue grew 48% in fiscal Q1 2027, ahead of management’s expectations. For fiscal Q2, management guided for even faster Azure growth of 49% to 50% at constant exchange rates. But some supply it expected in that quarter has moved out. So the company is counting on getting more work out of the chips it already runs to get there. The risk is not that customers walk away, but that Microsoft cannot serve them as fast as management has forecast. Microsoft Cloud, where Azure sits, brought in $63.9 billion of the company’s $92.3 billion in revenue in fiscal Q1 2027. So more than two thirds of the company’s sales come from Microsoft Cloud. Management said Microsoft Cloud’s growth accelerated to 30%. At that size, each 1% drop in Microsoft Cloud’s quarterly sales would be about $640 million. That is a drop in the sales themselves, not in their growth rate. Microsoft’s valuation is not near its own peak. The stock trades at 25.9 times its earnings over the past twelve months, against 21.5 for the S&P 500. Over the past 40 fiscal quarter ends, its multiple has run from 20.7 in June 2026 to 47.7 in December 2017. So the price appears to assume steady growth. It sits much nearer the bottom of that range than the top. Is Microsoft’s Supply Problem Only A Matter Of Timing? Based on what management has said, it mostly is. Demand remains intact, and the delayed contracts are now expected in the second half of the fiscal year. Management also expects free cash flow, the cash left after capital spending, to stay positive in fiscal 2027. It expects that even as capital spending speeds up in that half. The risk to a holder is a quarter or two of Azure growth below management’s forecast. Microsoft stock has also often fallen harder than the S&P 500 in rough markets. During the 2022 inflation shock and Fed tightening, the shares fell 32% against 24% for the index. They dropped 15% against 7.8% in the July to August 2024 yen shock. The supply problem amounts to a delay in serving customers rather than a loss of them. Microsoft is expected to report fiscal Q2 2027 results in January 2027. That release will show how Azure growth compares with the forecast management gave in October. Microsoft’s growth is real, yet the company still needs chips to arrive on time. The goal is to own that kind of growth without lying awake before every report. What If You Could Grow Wealth And Still Sleep At Night? Microsoft is 10% below its highest close of the past year. The company has detailed plans to add vast new capacity across its global network, a move that speaks directly to the question dominating the market this week: how quickly, and how durably, AI-infrastructure spending will keep scaling. For readers who follow Bluechip Stocks, Microsoft remains a closely watched name in the group. The expansion push builds on a stretch in which Microsoft's cloud arm has grown briskly, carried by enterprises moving workloads to Azure and by a wave of demand tied to generative-AI features woven across the company's software. Management has framed the added capacity as a response to that demand rather than a speculative bet, pointing to utilization across its data-center fleet as the reason more campuses are coming online. The backdrop into which this news landed has been unsettled. The artificial-intelligence trade is being tested after a sharp advance, semiconductor names have seesawed, and Federal Reserve meeting minutes have kept rate expectations in flux against a thin economic-data calendar. Sentiment has been choppy, and the market's front-running groups have rotated as traders reassess how much of the AI story is already priced in. Microsoft operates one of the broadest franchises in technology, spanning the Windows platform, the Office productivity suite, the Azure cloud, LinkedIn, the Dynamics business applications, security offerings and a gaming arm anchored by Xbox. That spread gives the company multiple engines of growth and a deep, recurring relationship with enterprises and consumers alike. Microsoft sits in a rare spot: it owns both the applications many organizations run every day and a growing share of the infrastructure those applications increasingly depend on. That dual position lets the company capture demand at several layers of the stack, from the software a worker touches to the servers humming in a distant data center, and it is the reason the name is treated as a core position within the broad market. The headline development is the scale of the capacity being added. Microsoft has outlined plans to expand its data-center fleet substantially, with new campuses designed around the power and cooling demands of dense AI computing. The build-out is a concrete expression of how the company expects demand to unfold, and it has become a focal point for a market trying to gauge the durability of the broader spending wave. Executing a build-out of this magnitude is an operational challenge in its own right. Sourcing components, securing power, constructing campuses on schedule and bringing capacity online efficiently all bear on how smoothly demand is met, and the market watches those details closely because they shape how quickly the company can convert surging interest into live services. The hyperscale race carries real challenges. Building at scale demands enormous capital, access to power and a steady supply of specialized chips, and any bottleneck in those inputs can slow the pace of expansion. Energy availability in particular has become a gating factor, with demand for electricity around data centers climbing even as grids strain to keep up. Microsoft competes with the other hyperscale cloud providers for enterprise workloads, with a wide field of software firms across productivity and business applications, and with a growing roster of AI specialists. What distinguishes its position is the way its software estate and its cloud infrastructure reinforce each other, so that demand for one tends to pull through demand for the other. Because of its size and its central role in the cloud and AI story, Microsoft functions as a barometer for enterprise technology spending as a whole. When the company signals that it is building capacity to meet demand, the market reads it as a vote of confidence in the durability of the AI transition, and that signal ripples across suppliers, power providers and the wider technology complex. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff. Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He's not saying he's replacing employees with AI, especially software engineers. He's saying he's reorganizing Microsoft into a company where everyone uses AI to do their work, and their jobs become focused on managing that AI. The buyout was "to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices," he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit. "Let's take software engineering. We went from, 'Well, we don't buy that AI can ever do software.' To suddenly, 'Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?' To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point," he explained. For some people, "that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?" he added, "but, I mean, it has to be done." He offered the example of the team that builds Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. He said the team consists of just 11 developers who have mastered using AI to do their jobs. "They build a software factory that builds the product. They don't build the product." He believes that every employee will one day similarly become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work. "That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs." But Microsoft, as a 51-year-old company, didn't grow up as an AI-first company. "So the question is, how quickly can an incumbent transform the work, the workflow, and the work artifact, and with all the wage support that goes with it?" he said. "It's going to take a bit more time than anyone expects. And there is going to be in all of this, you know, people who may say, 'Hey, I have some other choices I want to make.'" When asked about this same topic — why ask 60,000 people to voluntarily resign — last week by Gergely Orosz on his The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nadella further explained, "We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don't have control of their own destiny because the way we have talked about this AI revolution." He called out talk about the singularity (the hypothetical point at which AI surpasses human intelligence) and predictions that AI will take away all jobs. "All of that leads anyone who even wants to change to be sort of anxious … You have to sort of walk the hard walk of really making the structural changes, getting people slotted, giving them opportunity." In other words, the buyout was the message to employees: You can get with the new AI-first program, which will radically change your job, or you choose to get on with your life. Elsewhere. title: Intel Jumps on Foundry Win, Anthropic IPO & MSFT Deal - TradingPedia
content: Intel Corporation shares advanced 4.6% in pre-open trading after CEO Lip-Bu Tan announced at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin, Texas on Wednesday evening that the company had landed its first external customer for its advanced 18A chip manufacturing technology. The agreement marks a key step in Intel’s strategy to position itself as a serious player in contract chip manufacturing. The name of the customer was not revealed. However, Intel’s technology chief Pushkar Ranade specified that the deal covers the 18A-P manufacturing node, which entered risk production in June 2026. Intel’s pre-market strength was also supported by enthusiasm around Anthropic’s initial public offering. The AI company priced its shares at $83, above the $70-78 range it had marketed. The offering raised $81.3 billion and implied a valuation of about $1.5 trillion, described as the largest IPO on record. The scale and pricing of the IPO helped restore confidence in AI-related capital spending and sparked broad-based pre-market gains across semiconductor and hardware stocks. Momentum for Intel was further reinforced by an expanded long-term collaboration with Microsoft focused on Azure cloud and AI infrastructure. Under the updated partnership, Microsoft will become the first company to deploy Intel Foundry’s EMIB advanced packaging technology for its own Azure silicon. The companies also confirmed a multi-year supply agreement for Intel’s next-generation Xeon server processors, underscoring Intel’s importance within Microsoft’s data center and AI roadmap. Intel continued to execute on its restructuring agenda by launching another round of layoffs this week, targeting its global IT organization. The move contributed to investor confidence that CEO Lip-Bu Tan is maintaining a firm focus on cost control, a stance that markets have generally interpreted positively. The broader trading environment has been favorable to Intel’s move. U.S. equity futures pointed higher in pre-market activity, with the Nasdaq-100 leading the advance. Within technology and semiconductors, sentiment has been lifted by anticipation around Anthropic’s first day of trading on the Nasdaq and reduced anxiety over AI spending following strong results from sector peers earlier in the week. During today’s session, the S&P 500, Dow Jones, and Nasdaq indices were all trading in positive territory. Collectively, the new 18A foundry customer win, the strengthened Microsoft relationship, and the constructive macro and market backdrop have driven a sharp pre-market rise in Intel shares. The move offers a near-term boost for a stock that remains about 60% below its 52-week high of $142.35, as market participants continue to balance Intel’s longer-term turnaround efforts against ongoing challenges in PC demand and margin pressure. Azure is Microsoft's cloud computing platform and the main channel through which businesses access its AI services. For the first time, Microsoft disclosed Azure revenue as an exact dollar figure, giving investors clearer insight into the business. Microsoft moved from three reporting segments to two: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. The first includes Azure, its cloud productivity software and other business software. Microsoft averaged DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1 to score its coding claims. On that basis, MAI Code 2 delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol’s performance at 40% of the cost, according to Microsoft’s MAI Code 2 post. Against Claude Opus 5.5, it claims 96% at 5%. The post’s footnotes say MAI Code 2 costs are shown at a “50% promotional price.” Three of the four benchmarks ran on MSBench, Microsoft’s internal evaluation platform, using the GitHub Copilot CLI at maximum reasoning effort. At full price, the same figures put MAI Code 2 near 10% of Opus 5.5’s cost and 80% of GPT-6.1 Sol’s. OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Sol on 17 November, so Microsoft’s GPT comparison uses the previous version, Axios noted. Microsoft says the models are not yet tuned for fundamental science research or very long-horizon agentic work. MAI Code 2 is available on Copilot Pro, Pro+, Max, Business and Enterprise, and Code 2 Flash also reaches Free and Student users, according to GitHub’s changelog. Both are billed under usage-based billing. New models switch on automatically under the default policy unless an administrator disables them. Copilot usage is the figure for holders of Microsoft shares to watch, since Suleyman declined to set a traffic target for MAI Code 2 but predicted significant adoption, Axios reported. Axios wrote that the integration could move some coding workloads away from outside models. Microsoft shares now carry an in-house coding model inside GitHub Copilot, which Microsoft says costs 5% of Claude Opus 5.5 at a promotional price. Anthropic priced above its $70 to $78 range, valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion fully diluted, and trades on Nasdaq as ANT from 19 November, TechCrunch reported. Azure grew 48% in the quarter to 30 September, beating the 45% Microsoft had guided. Cheaper in-house models bear directly on margins behind Microsoft shares as investors question AI data center spending. The Zhitong Finance APP learned that Morgan Stanley released a research report, reiterating its "Overweight" rating on Microsoft (MSFT.US) with a price target of $650. The Morgan Stanley analyst team led by Adam Wood stated that after Microsoft held its Ignite conference in San Francisco and interacted with CEO Nadella and CFO Amy Hood, the firm believes Microsoft is one of the few software companies that have already realized returns on their AI investments. Computing Power Strategy: Avoid blindly maximizing long-term GPU contracts; maintain diversified computing power service offerings. In its report, Morgan Stanley noted that, in allocating computing resources, Microsoft's management treats GPUs as modular assets and refrains from blindly pursuing long-term GPU-as-a-Service (GPUaaS) contracts. Management stated that the company will proactively reserve computing capacity to serve its own first-party products, the Foundry platform, and external enterprise customers, rather than locking all resources into long-term agreements. From Microsoft's perspective, model labs are merely key clients and do not represent the entirety of its cloud business; maintaining elastic computing capacity is a proactive investment in the value of its own platforms and applications, aimed at capturing monetization opportunities for high-value-added services built on top of its infrastructure. Regarding the market's attention to the Neocloud architecture strategy, Microsoft stated that its underlying strategy has not changed; the priority remains building its own data centers, followed by a long-term leasing model in which Microsoft controls data center fit-out, networking, and hardware equipment. This approach allows for better management of data center operational efficiency, deployment pace, and capital expenditures on equipment. The cancellation of some third-party partnership orders stems from suppliers' inadequate service performance, rather than a shift in Microsoft's overall computing power procurement strategy, nor does it signify a major change in the market's computing power supply-and-demand dynamics. Meanwhile, Microsoft's improvements in computing efficiency are not limited to the GPU level; CPU utilization and the storage system are also key focuses of optimization. Moreover, the newly deployed infrastructure inherits this optimization strategy, so the efficiency gains are not confined to existing server clusters. However, the bank cautions that efficiency gains should not be treated as an independent upward variable in computing capacity planning; rather, efficiency improvements can simultaneously boost revenue-carrying capacity and reduce delivery costs. Profitability and Gross Margin: Improvements at the product level take precedence, while the cloud business mix will temporarily weigh on the overall gross margin. Morgan Stanley specifically pointed out a key point that is easily confused by the market: Microsoft's management team's core objective is to improve the gross margins of Azure and M365 individually; the overall gross margin for Microsoft Cloud disclosed in the financial report is merely a result of business development, not a direct performance metric for management. Even if the profitability of individual products continues to improve, once the proportion of the high-growth but relatively low-margin Azure business keeps expanding, it will still dilute Microsoft's cloud consolidated gross margin. Investors should not simply conclude that the profitability of individual cloud services is weakening just because the overall gross margin is under pressure. When assessing future profit improvements, the focus should be on tracking resource utilization, infrastructure efficiency, model operating costs, and the consumption scale of high-value platform services. Enterprise AI Flywheel: Positioned as a multi-model orchestration layer, it is not limited to in-house large models; Microsoft IQ closes the capability loop. Microsoft does not bet its competitiveness on a single model; the core value for enterprise customers lies in the entire ecosystem surrounding the model: enterprise business context, model scheduling framework, memory capabilities, and secure, trustworthy governance. Enterprises can mix cutting-edge large models, Microsoft's self-developed specialized MAI models, and open-source weight models. The Microsoft platform is responsible for selecting the most cost-effective model based on task requirements to get the job done, while keeping control of enterprise business data with the customer and providing unified management of the security, permissions, and cost expenditures of all AI agents. At this conference, Microsoft IQ was unveiled, integrating Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, and Web IQ, further connecting the entire enterprise AI flywheel and tightly coupling business data, model orchestration, and application distribution. Morgan Stanley believes that the more models available on the market, the higher the strategic value of Microsoft as a platform layer that bridges models and enterprise business workflows. Copilot Commercialization: Dual-Drive Model of Subscriptions and Pay-as-You-Go, with Early Adoption in Non-Code Scenarios Microsoft has adopted a hybrid business model that combines subscription-based pricing with usage-based billing: subscriptions provide stable base revenue, while usage-based billing generates incremental income in line with customers' actual AI workloads. Management disclosed that some large customers have already spent more on the Copilot Cowork product than on Microsoft's other products combined; however, the CFO team emphasized that this case is an extreme outlier and not representative of the broader customer base. Moreover, the product suite has only recently been commercialized, so it is still too early to establish reliable expectations for adoption rates. Currently, Copilot's adoption in coding-related workflows is strong, but consumer use across broader knowledge‑work scenarios remains in the early stages of development. While growth potential is significant, the pace of real‑world deployment remains a key uncertainty. Drawing an analogy to Azure's early development, management notes that as enterprises embrace AI agents, their demand for cost control and transparent spending is particularly pronounced. Microsoft has launched Agent 365, a business analytics and cost-management tool that ties AI expenditures to operational outcomes and budgetary alerts, helping companies manage fluctuating AI usage and remove barriers to large-scale deployment. However, the direct revenue generated by this suite of tools depends on the pace at which enterprises expand production-grade AI workloads. In-house chip strategy: Maia and Cobalt serve as efficiency supplements; not all workloads are migrated to in-house hardware. Microsoft's custom chips are part of a diversified computing fleet and do not aim to migrate all workloads to in-house hardware. Take the Maia AI chip and the newly released Cobalt 200 as examples: the Cobalt 200 targets agent-based AI workloads, delivering up to 50% better performance than its predecessor, the Cobalt 100. Microsoft will continue to procure chips from external vendors; the goal of its in-house chips is to enhance performance and reduce costs in specific scenarios, serving as a complementary lever for overall computing efficiency rather than an exclusive replacement. This approach continues the earlier trend of diversifying computing chips from a single source—Intel (INTC.US)—to include AMD (AMD.US) and Cobalt. The takeaway is straightforward: professional coverage still leans constructive, but the stock is not being valued as a straight-line story from here. The chart structure is softer than the fundamental backdrop. MSFT is below its SMA 7 at $517.80, SMA 20 at $525.30, SMA 50 at $527.86, EMA 12 at $520.75 and EMA 26 at $524.12. That bearish alignment suggests overhead supply remains in control until price can reclaim the low-to-mid $520s. At the same time, the longer-term trend is still intact: the SMA 200 sits at $462.80, well below the current quote. RSI at 45.05 is neutral, not oversold, and MACD is negative, which fits a market that is cooling rather than collapsing. Bollinger positioning also leaves room for both sides: the lower band is $503.31, the middle band is $525.30 and the upper band is $547.30. Key levels from the tape are clear: immediate resistance is $521.40, stronger resistance is $527.27, pivot is $511.58, immediate support is $505.71 and strong support is $495.89. With ATR(14) at $13.79, normal daily swings are wide enough that a test of support or resistance can happen fast once volume picks up. Binance perpetual futures data is leaning defensive but not extreme. The funding rate is -0.1909%, which means shorts are paying longs, and the global long/short ratio is 0.7212 with 41.9% long and 58.1% short accounts. Top traders show a similar tilt at 0.7262, with 42.1% long and 57.9% short. That does not prove bearish conviction on the stock itself; it only shows Binance cohorts are positioned more to the short side in this contract. The open interest read is also important. Real-time open interest stands at 37,082.14 contracts, daily OI value is $19.46 million, and 24-hour OI is down 5.55%. That combination usually points to position reduction rather than fresh leverage being added. On the other hand, taker flow over the last hour shows aggressive buying pressure, with a taker buy/sell ratio of 2.3137. In plain terms, price is sitting in a tug-of-war: short positioning is heavier, but buyers are still stepping in on the tape. If MSFT can reclaim the $521.40 to $527.27 zone with better volume, the chart would start to look more constructive and the market would have room to challenge the Bollinger middle band and then the upper band. If it loses $505.71, the next test is the $503.31 lower Bollinger band, then $495.89. A break below that would weaken the current structure materially and put the long-term trend support at $462.80 back on the table. With chip and AI-infrastructure names swinging sharply and the week's marquee semiconductor earnings print framing sentiment, a hyperscale operator of Microsoft's stature sits at the heart of the debate. The expansion push builds on a stretch in which Microsoft's cloud arm has grown briskly, carried by enterprises moving workloads to Azure and by a wave of demand tied to generative-AI features woven across the company's software. That framing matters because the market has grown wary of the scale of AI-linked spending. The context is also competitive. The backdrop into which this news landed has been unsettled. The artificial-intelligence trade is being tested after a sharp advance, semiconductor names have seesawed, and Federal Reserve meeting minutes have kept rate expectations in flux against a thin economic-data calendar. Within that mix, a diversified mega-cap that spans productivity software, cloud infrastructure, gaming and security reads differently from a lone-product name. Microsoft operates among the broadest franchises in technology, spanning the Windows platform, the Office productivity suite, the Azure cloud, LinkedIn, the Dynamics business applications, security offerings and a gaming arm anchored by Xbox. That spread gives the company multiple engines of growth and a deep, recurring relationship with enterprises and consumers alike. At the center of the current story sits Azure, the cloud platform that rents computing, storage and a widening catalog of AI services to organizations of every size. The data-center network underpinning Azure spans regions across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia-Pacific, and the current expansion aims to deepen that map with new campuses tuned for the heavy demands of AI workloads. Beyond infrastructure, Microsoft has threaded generative-AI features across its software, from coding assistants to productivity copilots, turning its vast installed base into a distribution channel for new capabilities. That combination of platform reach and infrastructure scale is what gives the company its distinctive standing in the AI era. Readers following Bluechip Stocks can place this update within its wider category. Microsoft sits in a rare spot: it owns both the applications many organizations run every day and a growing share of the infrastructure those applications increasingly depend on. That dual position lets the company capture demand at several layers of the stack, from the software a worker touches to the servers humming in a distant data center, and it is the reason the name is treated as a core position within the broad market. As a cornerstone of the wider US Bluechip Stocks that traders follow, Microsoft is frequently read as a proxy for enterprise technology spending and for the health of the cloud transition. The headline development is the scale of the capacity being added. Microsoft has outlined plans to expand its data-center fleet substantially, with new campuses designed around the power and cooling demands of dense AI computing. The build-out is a concrete expression of how the company expects demand to unfold, and it has become a focal point for a market trying to gauge the durability of the broader spending wave. The company has also continued to broaden its own family of AI models and services, extending the menu that Azure customers can reach for. That deepening catalog strengthens the pull of the platform and reinforces the link between Microsoft's software reach and its infrastructure scale. Sourcing components, securing power, constructing campuses on schedule and bringing capacity online efficiently all bear on how smoothly demand is met, and the market watches those details closely because they shape how quickly the company can convert surging interest into live services. Capital discipline is the other side of the ledger. Keeping that balance steady is central to how the model performs through the current cycle, and it is a thread traders return to whenever the scale of AI spending is debated.
